content: Angina pectoris refers to chest pain or discomfort that arises when the heart muscle does not receive an adequate supply of blood. This pain is often described as a sensation of pressure or squeezing in the chest. It may also radiate to the shoulders, arms, neck, jaw, or back. In some cases, it can mimic the feeling of indigestion. Angina is not a disease itself but rather a symptom of coronary artery disease (CAD), which is the most common type of heart disease. CAD occurs when fatty deposits, known as plaque, accumulate in the coronary arteries, reducing blood flow. This diminished blood flow prevents the heart muscle from receiving sufficient oxygen-rich blood, leading to angina. Symptoms of Angina Pectoris The hallmark symptom of angina is chest pain, which serves as a warning sign of myocardial ischemia. However, other symptoms may accompany angina, including: Chest pain: This is typically localized to the precordial region or behind the sternum. It is important to note that not all chest pain is related to coronary artery disease. Chest pressure: Some individuals describe this as a sensation of a heavy weight or a tight band around the chest. Indigestion-like symptoms: Loss of appetite, nausea, or vomiting may occur in some patients. Pain radiating to other areas: Discomfort may extend to the shoulders, arms, jaw, or back, often accompanying chest pain. It is crucial to recognize that other health conditions can cause similar symptoms. Only a healthcare professional can accurately diagnose the underlying cause. Anyone experiencing these symptoms should consult a doctor promptly to ensure early diagnosis and treatment. Risk Factors for Angina Several factors increase the risk of developing angina, many of which overlap with the risk factors for coronary artery disease. These can be categorized into modifiable and non-modifiable risk factors: Modifiable Risk Factors 1. Cigarette smoking: Smoking significantly increases the risk of coronary heart disease, with smokers being 2–4 times more likely to develop the condition compared to non-smokers. Smoking also doubles the risk of sudden cardiac death in individuals with coronary heart disease. 2. High blood cholesterol: Elevated cholesterol levels, particularly LDL cholesterol, are strongly associated with an increased risk of coronary artery disease. Diet plays a significant role in cholesterol levels. 3. Stress: Chronic stress can contribute to unhealthy behaviors such as overeating or smoking, which in turn increase the risk of cardiovascular diseases. 4. Obesity: A high body mass index (BMI), particularly above 28, is a risk factor for angina. Weight management can help reduce this risk. 5. Hypertension: High blood pressure reduces the coronary arteries' reserve capacity, increasing the likelihood of coronary artery disease. 6. Diabetes mellitus: Diabetes damages both coronary arteries and myocardial capillaries, raising the risk of coronary artery disease. 7. Excessive alcohol consumption: Overconsumption of alcohol can harm the arteries and myocardium. Non-Modifiable Risk Factors 1. Age: Individuals over the age of 65 are at a higher risk of developing coronary artery disease. 2. Gender: Men are at a higher risk than women, although post-menopausal women also face an increased risk compared to younger women. 3. Family history: A family history of cardiovascular diseases increases the likelihood of developing coronary artery disease. 4. Race: African Americans are at a higher risk compared to other racial groups. Diagnosis of Angina Since other health conditions can mimic the symptoms of angina, it is essential to undergo a thorough evaluation by a healthcare professional. Diagnostic tests may include: Electrocardiogram (ECG): This painless test measures the heart's electrical activity to detect abnormalities or irregular heart rhythms. Echocardiogram: This imaging test identifies areas of the heart that may not be contracting normally. Blood tests: Tests such as CK-MB and troponin levels can help determine if the heart has sustained damage. Coronary angiography: This imaging procedure involves injecting a special dye into the coronary arteries to visualize blockages on X-rays. Stress testing: Conducted during physical exertion, this test helps identify heart disease more effectively. When to Seek Urgent Medical Care Individuals with a family history of cardiovascular diseases or unhealthy lifestyle habits should regularly consult their doctor for follow-up care. Immediate medical attention is necessary if any of the following symptoms occur: Persistent and severe chest pain Sudden drop in blood pressure Shortness of breath Angina or chest pain accompanied by sweating, nausea, or discomfort in the shoulders, arms, jaw, neck, or abdomen These symptoms may indicate acute coronary syndrome (ACS), which requires urgent evaluation and treatment. Treatment Options for Angina Treatment for angina includes general lifestyle modifications, medications, and interventional or surgical procedures. The choice of treatment depends on the severity of symptoms and the degree of coronary artery stenosis. A doctor will discuss the available options, expected outcomes, and potential side effects to develop a personalized treatment plan. General Therapy Weight and waistline management Smoking and alcohol cessation Regular physical activity Stress management Medications 1. Anti-platelet drugs: Low-dose aspirin (75–100 mg daily) is beneficial for most patients with stable angina. Alternatives like clopidogrel or prasugrel may be used for those with contraindications to aspirin. 2. Beta-blockers: These reduce heart rate, myocardial contractility, and oxygen demand. Commonly used agents include metoprolol, bisoprolol, and nebivolol. Beta-blockers are contraindicated in patients with asthma, severe conduction block, or heart failure. 3. Nitroglycerin (NG): This vasodilator improves myocardial ischemia and is available in various forms, including sublingual tablets, sprays, and transdermal patches. Side effects may include headache, hypotension, and facial flushing. 4. Calcium-channel blockers: These reduce myocardial oxygen demand and reverse coronary vasospasm. Verapamil and gallopamil are commonly used, with bradycardia being a potential side effect. 5. ACE inhibitors: Drugs like enalapril and ramipril improve heart failure symptoms and prognosis. Side effects include dry cough and angioedema. Patients intolerant to ACE inhibitors may switch to angiotensin II receptor antagonists. 6. Statins: These cholesterol-lowering agents reduce LDL cholesterol and increase HDL cholesterol. Common drugs include atorvastatin and fluvastatin. Side effects may include liver enzyme abnormalities and muscle pain. Percutaneous Coronary Intervention (PCI) PCI involves using a catheter to open blocked coronary arteries with a balloon or stent. This procedure improves coronary blood flow and alleviates angina symptoms. It is performed in a cardiac catheterization lab and is considered safe and effective. Coronary Artery Bypass Grafting (CABG) CABG is a surgical procedure that reroutes blood flow around blocked coronary arteries using healthy blood vessels from the patient’s body. Post-surgery, patients are advised to adopt a low-fat, low-cholesterol diet and engage in regular physical activity to prevent further blockages. Where to Seek Medical Care Patients experiencing symptoms of angina should seek care at hospitals equipped to treat cardiovascular conditions. Early diagnosis and treatment are essential to prevent complications. Diseases with Similar Symptoms Other conditions may mimic angina symptoms, necessitating careful evaluation by a healthcare provider: Shortness of breath: May be caused by respiratory diseases like pneumonia or tuberculosis. Indigestion: Could indicate digestive disorders such as gastritis or peptic ulcers. Pain in shoulders, arms, jaw, or back: May result from conditions like scapulohumeral periarthritis or dental issues.
